title: Nonsense vs Nothingness: The great philosophical divide
subtitle: Bridging the analytic-continental rift
author: Simone Mahrenholz
introduction: There is a great divide running through philosophy. Analytic versus Continental. The proponents of each see their version of philosophy as more valid and cast doubt on the legitimacy of the other. Philosopher Simone Mahrenholz here argues this divide is the product of contingent events in history. Tracing the origins of both schools in part to outstanding personalities in early 20th-century Germany and Europe, in conjunction with world-political developments, she reveals this rift in philosophy as caused and radicalized by a peculiar course of events, including the rise of Hitler.
body:
Newcomers to contemporary academic philosophy might find themselves at times perplexed by the degree and vehemence with which the discipline is still divided at most philosophy departments in the world. The current distinction between so called “analytic” and “continental” philosophy is at the latest a product of the 1970s, its methodological foundations however, have their origin in the 1920s or earlier. And, strictly speaking, it is a false equivalent: relating a method, analytic, to a region, the European continent. One could talk instead of Anglo-American versus European philosophy, or of analytic versus historical methods. But both of these would be misleading. Authors subsumed under “continental” are not predominantly historical in orientation, yet they include historical investigations for inquiries into their fields. “Analytic” philosophers, in contrast, tend to dismiss discourses from previous centuries as overcome by – well – scientific progress. They self-identify via the ideals of exactness and clarity and the method of logical analysis: of concepts, arguments, language and their relation to reality. Also, hardly any conference call or job posting goes out without explicit reference to methodological “rigour”.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The matrix, myths, and metaphysics With Hilary Lawson, Joanna Kavenna, Becky Parker, Eric Weinstein

What method, then, complements “analytic” on the continental side? This depends partly on whom you ask. The large, heterogeneous group under this umbrella includes German idealism, phenomenology, existentialism, critical theory, (post-)structuralism, as well as their predecessors, such as Kierkegaard, Nietzsche and many others. We often find a tendency here to engage in meta-philosophical self-reflection, alongside an awareness of the historical emergence of those concepts, actions and values that seem to be naturally given.

Without Ludwig Wittgenstein, Martin Heidegger and Adolf Hitler, all born within the same five months of the year 1889 and a radius of 380 miles, the face of academic philosophy would most likely look quite different.

Yet, the distinction between the two schools is everything but clear-cut, and many philosophers defy or try to overcome it altogether. Nonetheless, students who want to study the Anglo-American canon alongside authors from Europe, let alone non-Western traditions, will often find themselves sent away. Those interested in Nietzsche, Foucault, Merleau-Ponty, Deleuze, Derrida or even Hegel, Husserl, Heidegger, Sartre or de Beauvoir, will at most Universities switch to other departments: Religious Studies, French, English or German Studies, Gender Studies, Comparative Studies, history and more.

This remarkable status quo is the product of an extraordinary confluence of economic, world-political, socio-historical events on the one hand, and a small handful of wilful, determined, highly influential and idiosyncratic personalities on the other. Without Ludwig Wittgenstein, Martin Heidegger and Adolf Hitler, all born within the same five months of the year 1889 and a radius of 380 miles, the face of academic philosophy would most likely look quite different.

Philosophy as science or as pseudo-science? Nothingness meets Nonsense

Let us zoom into the year 1929 in Germany: a country in between two World Wars, governed by the young, fragile democracy of the Weimar Republic. Martin Heidegger, married father of two, had been recently appointed full professor at the University of Freiburg as the successor of his teacher Edmund Husserl. He had fought a long and frustrating fight towards a permanent professorship; what finally decided the issue was the publication of Being and Time in 1927, followed by the retirement of Husserl. His growing visibility got an extra boost through his famous 1929 debate with the renowned neo-Kantian Ernst Cassirer at a prestigious summer course in Davos, Switzerland, where people also witnessed amicable conversations between Heidegger and his soon-to-become combatant Rudolf Carnap. A few weeks later, Heidegger held his famous inaugural speech at Freiburg University, entitled “What is metaphysics?”  In this lecture, Heidegger describes his view of the scientific attitude in philosophy. He stresses two points in particular. Metaphysics must cover “the whole” of what-is, including the common ground of the individual sciences. And it must include the role of the philosophising subject or scientist itself into the scientific inquiry.

“The questioner as such is by his very question involved in the question. (…) Man – one entity among others – ‘pursues’ science. In this ‘pursuit’ what happens is (…) the irruption of a particular entity called ‘Man’ into the whole of what-is – such that, in and through this irruption, what-is manifests itself as and how it is.”

This move, combining elements of Kant’s constructivism with Husserl’s phenomenology, stands in stark opposition to the rivaling logical positivist movement of his time. Heidegger’s strategy aimed to reveal the internal contradictions and shortcomings of that logical-analytic and empiricist “scientism”. In particular, he puts the ideal of objectivity under scrutiny. In a classical dialectical move, Heidegger begins his discourse from seemingly firm scientific ground only to steer it into surprising terrain:

“The distinction of science lies in the fact that, in a specific manner, it and it alone allows the object itself the first and last word. In this objectivity of questioning, of definition and proof, there is a certain limited submission to what-is, so that it may reveal itself. This submissive attitude taken up by scientific theory becomes the basis of (…) the possibility for science to acquire its leadership. (…) What is to be investigated is Being only and nothing else; being alone and further – nothing; solely Being, and beyond being – nothing. What about this Nothing? (…) Does the Nothing exist only because the Not, i.e. the Negation, exists? Or is it the other way around? (…) We assert: the Nothing is prior to the Notand the Negation. (…) We know the Nothing. (…) Anxiety reveals the Nothing. (…) The Nothing itself nothings.”

The whole speech, and these sentences in particular, caused a major stir, provoking alternatingly mockery, admiration, contempt, idolatry, suspicion and natural feelings of logical and moral superiority. In a way, Heidegger seemed to display a unique sense for branding with this quasi-ruthless violation of the rules of language and common sense. The talk further presented a whole casuistry of Nothingness, with references to undirected Angst or boredom, the pains of refusal, loathing, prohibitions and of feeling drawn into the abyss of our own non-existence. In a country that had just emerged from the first world war and already displayed signs of a new upcoming crisis, Heidegger’s words were alternatingly seductive and alarming. His “disintegrating” of logic “in the vortex of a more original questioning” seemed compelling to some, as well as repulsive, if not dangerous, to others. The divide was already in full swing.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Lost in language With Rufus Duits, Hilary Lawson, Barry C. Smith, Maria Balaska

A philosophical anti-bullshit detector

Heidegger’s speech was in a way a major gift to the Vienna circle: an interdisciplinary group of thinkers formed in the 1920s in Vienna around the philosopher and physicist Moritz Schlick and including Rudolf Carnap, Otto Neurath and many others. Their programmatic efforts towards an exact philosophy, modeled after the exact sciences, contains much of what developed later as “analytic” philosophy. The interdisciplinary group had read and discussed Wittgenstein’s Tractatus Logico-philosophicus religiously. Together with Bertrand Russell’s plea for a logical-analytic method, the book offered them well-tailored argumentative tools against a “metaphysics” that transcended the empirical or logical terrain. The Vienna circle’s manifesto “The Scientific Conception of the World” from 1929, co-written by Carnap, Otto Neurath and the mathematician Hans Hahn, can be seen as an oscillation in spirit between the two strange attractors Heidegger and Wittgenstein, as the negative and positive poles.

In the spirit of positivism and empiricism, philosophy should be held accountable to the principle of verification and falsification – quite in contrast to traditional metaphysics. Heidegger had warned of reducing reality to science, logic and the merely empirical.

Wittgenstein’s Tractatus however, first published in 1921, is a text so unusual that allegedly not even his mentor Bertrand Russell, author of the preface to the English edition, understood it, at least according to Wittgenstein. It consists of seven numbered sentences, each accompanied with annotations, except for the last one. Like any good symphony or speech, it begins and ends deceptively laconically:

  1. The world is everything that is the case.
  2. Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.

In between, we find a methodological programme, discussions of the nature and foundations of mathematical logic, postulates regarding the relation of language and world, saying as opposed to showing and numerous references to boundaries or limits: of logic, of the world, of what can be said clearly in logical propositions and hence of what can be thought. Sense and nonsense are frequently mentioned in the text. As Wittgenstein says in the preface:

“The book will draw a limit to thinking, or rather, not to thinking, but to the expression of thoughts (…). The limit can, therefore, only be drawn in language, and what lies on the other side of the limit will be simply nonsense.”

Analysing logical fallacies in language becomes the key for dissolving philosophical problems. In accordance with Russell’s program, the book warns of involuntary nonsense-production by overstepping logical boundaries.

“What can be said at all, can be said clearly” – this claim from the preface was adopted as a motto by the Vienna circle. In the spirit of positivism and empiricism, philosophy should be held accountable to the principle of verification and falsification – quite in contrast to traditional metaphysics. Heidegger had warned of reducing reality to science, logic and the merely empirical. The Vienna circle in contrast warned of stepping out of the realms of science, logic and the empirical: seen as the touchstones of clarity, common sense and progress in the sense of the Enlightenment. All in all, they had a comprehensive and ambitious vision:

“The vitality that shows itself in the efforts for a rational transformation of the social and economic order, permeates (…) a scientific world-conception too. (…) Neatness and clarity are striven for, and dark distances and unfathomable depths rejected. In science there are no ‘depths’, there is surface everywhere. (…) Everything is accessible to man; and man is the measure of all things. (…)The method of clarification is logical analysis of it”. (Scientific World Conception)

Based on this, Carnap prepared meticulously for a more targeted attack. In his article “The Elimination of Metaphysics through Logical Analysis of Language” from 1931, he quotes Heidegger’s passages on “Nothing” as an outstanding example of metaphysical nonsense. Within the framework of a rigorous logical analysis, he disqualifies these claims as “pseudo-statements”, culminating in a remarkable expression of pent-up aggression:

“when a metaphysician gives verbal expression to his dualistic-heroic attitude towards life (…), is it not perhaps because he lacks the ability of a Beethoven to express this attitude in an adequate medium? Metaphysicians are musicians without musical ability.” (Carnap, Overcoming Metaphysics)

In that time, the worst thing one could accuse a philosopher of being was an artist, let alone an untalented one.

Which side are you on? – Wittgenstein’s double-take on nonsense

Carnap felt this cancellation of metaphysics to be in direct alignment with Wittgenstein’s Tractatus. However, Wittgenstein’s own attitude towards nonsense is less clear-cut. In fact, at some point in the book, the whole corpus of the Tractatus falls under its own verdict of being nonsense, or the sense-less, creating a telling paradox.

“Anyone who understands me (…) must, so to speak, throw away the ladder after he has climbed up on it. He must transcend these propositions as nonsensical, and then he will see the world aright.” (6.54)

It seems to be impossible to demarcate a certain boundary of sense without taking refuge to a crossing of the line towards the logically dubious. Certain regions can only be indicated indirectly. As Wittgenstein wrote in a 1919 letter to his editor Ludwig von Ficker:

“My work consists of two parts: the one presented here plus all that I have not written. And it is precisely this second part that is the important one.”

Unlike his Vienna followers, Wittgenstein’s interest in the boundaries of sense and world clearly included the other side.

“I’ve managed in my book to put everything firmly into place by being silent about it”, he remarks in the same letter to Ficker. Philosophy “should limit the unthinkable from within through the thinkable. (4114) It will mean the Unsayable by clearly presenting the Sayable. (4.115) There is indeed the Unsayable. This shows itself; it is the mystical.” (6.522)

Philosophy will mean the Unsayable – which shows itself. There is indeed sound in this “silence”. However, it was not only the Vienna circle that didn’t hear it. His mentor Russell apparently didn’t either, as a letter by Wittgenstein suggests:

“I’m afraid you haven’t really got hold of my main contention, to which the whole business of logical propositions is only a corollary. The main point is the theory of what can be expressed [gesagt] by propositions – i.e. by language – (and, which comes to the same, what can be thought) and what cannot be expressed by propositions, but only shown [gezeigt]; which, I believe, is the cardinal problem of philosophy.” (letter from August 1918)

Political petrifications

The events leading to the contemporary rift between philosophical schools extend over the period of the two world wars. WWI was in full swing when Wittgenstein wrote his Tractatus, completed in 1918. Less than ten years later, the presages of WWII were already visible. 1929, the turbulent year of Davos, of Heidegger’s What is Metaphysics and of the Vienna circle’s counter-manifesto Scientific World View, was also the year of “bloody May” (Blutmai) when, during a violent first of May communist demonstration in Berlin, the police killed 33 innocent bystanders. And it was the year of the Wall Street crash and its subsequent global economic crisis, with dire consequences for the German population. The omnipresent crises facilitated Hitler’s rise to power in January 1933, which also led to Heidegger’s election as Rector at Freiburg University, followed by his publicly embracing Hitler’s ideology and joining the Nazi party.

Thus almost overnight, the alternative between philosophy as an “exact” logical science and a Heidegger-style metaphysics assumed a new and urgent political and ethical dimension. For many, it was associated with the question of life and death. In this way, Hitler’s rise deepened and petrified the rift within philosophy.

Heidegger’s becoming a Nazi led to ongoing debates over whether his philosophical system contains at its roots fascist and anti-Semitic essences. The sounds of metaphysics and any darker or higher notes in it were as of now suspect: as the flute tones of evil. Not only colleagues like Gilbert Ryle, who had originally written a respectful if not glowing review of Being and Time, subsequently referred to Heidegger's political role in several scathing public denigrations of his thought, as the work of a "bad man". Metaphysics now found itself on the far right. The members of the Vienna circle, on the other hand, over half of whom were Jewish, contained social democrats and their references included also Karl Marx.

Thus almost overnight, the alternative between philosophy as an “exact” logical science and a Heidegger-style metaphysics assumed a new and urgent political and ethical dimension. For many, it was associated with the question of life and death. In this way, Hitler’s rise deepened and petrified the rift within philosophy. Further, the forced emigration of Jewish, socialist and other members of society exported the divide and dispersed it throughout the globe. Rudolf Carnap and other Vienna circle members, as well as representatives of what became later “continental” philosophy, such as Theodor W. Adorno from the Frankfurt School, emigrated to the United States.

SUGGESTED READING Heidegger vs Carnap: The metaphysics of nothing By Roy Sorensen

Epilogue: Towards bridging the divide

As is well known, Wittgenstein grew up in a household where artists such as Johannes Brahms came regularly for tea. It might be no accident that the philosopher who first presented crucial impulses in bridging the philosophical divide was Susanne K. Langer, daughter of German emigrees, trained musician and a highly respected analytic philosopher at Harvard University already at a young age. Having studied with Alfred North Whitehead and authored one of the first textbooks on symbolic logic, Langer had clearly perceived the sounds in Wittgenstein’s “silence”. Familiar also with Ernst Cassirer’s theory of “symbolic forms”, she introduced in her book Philosophy in a New Key (1942) the distinction between “discursive” and “presentative” forms, partly to clarify Wittgenstein’s saying-showing difference. Discursive forms include language and formal logic, presentative forms in contrast gestures, music and pictorial systems.

“The "elements" that the camera or painting represents are not the ‘elements’ that language represents. They are a thousand times more numerous”. (Langer, PNK 95)

They are often also more nuanced, fine-grained and potentially more precise. Langer claimed, against Carnap and Russell, that these symbolizations are not simply emotive or expressive but symbolic forms in their own right, with characteristic cognitive functions.

What used to reside on the philosophical margins, as “not really philosophy”, is currently moving more and more to its centre. A symptom of this is the rising status of aesthetics, or philosophy of art.

It was the logician Nelson Goodman who saw the huge implications of Langer’s conceptual moves. In Languages of Art, published in 1968, he created a “General Theory of Symbols” that rests on several crucial points from Langer, unifying them within an elegant and sparse symbol-logical system. He also introduced the term “density” into the logical terrain, meaning the “continuous” or “analog”, a move which allowed for the logical analysis of artworks especially. This went hand in hand with Goodman’s then revolutionarily wide concept of “cognition”, which explicitly includes the emotive as well as sense perception – against all “analytic” odds.

Langer and Goodman are often described as unifying “analytic” and “continental” features in philosophy, bridging the gap. They subscribe to logical analysis as a methodological keystone, while opening up the fields of philosophical analysis to domains and faculties long located outside of analytic philosophy, previously seen as "mere" art, ethics or simply as expressing subjective attunements.

Following these pioneers, we are now in the middle of changes within the philosophical academic scene. What used to reside on the philosophical margins, as “not really philosophy”, is currently moving more and more to its centre.  A symptom of this is the rising status of aesthetics, or philosophy of art. Among graduate students at philosophy departments, aesthetics as a field of research has become increasingly hot. Or cool. Understanding our interaction with and through the arts means exploring our faculties and cognitive domains in increasingly sophisticated ways.

Which includes, by the way, Wittgenstein’s “unspeakable”. Doing aesthetics implies crossing the boundary – but only to re-install it elsewhere, highlighting new, illuminating distinctions. Apropos boundaries: philosophically analyzing the arts also helps with conceptually approaching “the Nothing”. Here, we might consult another provenly unmusical musician. But on Nietzsche, and his role in all this, another time.
